subject: operating-systems
title: User mode and kernel mode
summary: Processor privilege modes restrict ordinary application code from executing privileged operations and protect the kernel.

resources.title: Kernel (operating system)
resources.why: Covers kernel responsibilities, protection, resource management, and hardware access.

resources.title: intro(2): Introduction to system calls
resources.why: Explains kernel entry points, library wrappers, mode transitions, and error reporting.

questions.prompt: On a typical protected CPU, which mode permits privileged instructions that alter hardware-control state?
options: Kernel mode
A mode entered by every function call
Text mode
User mode
questions.answerKey: Kernel mode has elevated privileges; user mode restricts access to privileged instructions.
questions.explanation: Ordinary function calls do not automatically change privilege level.

questions.prompt: Why does a conventional system call enter kernel mode and later return to user mode?
options: The transition guarantees the requested operation succeeds
The application executable must be recompiled after every request
The service needs controlled kernel privileges, but the application should not retain them
The transition permanently makes the process an administrator
questions.answerKey: The controlled entry lets trusted kernel code perform a privileged service, then returns to restricted execution; the request may still fail.
questions.explanation: A system call is not permanent privilege escalation and does not guarantee success.

questions.prompt: A program adds two integers stored in its own memory and executes no privileged instruction. What normally happens to privilege mode during the addition?
options: It enters kernel mode for each arithmetic instruction
It stays in user mode
It enters kernel mode and remains there until process exit
It switches to disk-controller mode
questions.answerKey: Ordinary arithmetic over the process's own memory runs in user mode; a kernel transition is not needed for every instruction.
questions.explanation: Not every instruction passes through the kernel.

questions.prompt: A user-mode program attempts to execute a privileged instruction directly. What normally happens on a protected architecture?
options: The OS permanently disables memory protection
The instruction is automatically converted to read()
The CPU silently grants kernel privileges
The CPU raises a protection exception or fault
questions.answerKey: Privilege checks reject the instruction in user mode and transfer control through the architecture's exception mechanism.
questions.explanation: A privileged instruction is not automatically a valid system call.

questions.prompt: An engineer proposes running every application in kernel mode to reduce transition overhead. Which is the most important downside?
options: Every application would become memory-safe
CPU scheduling would become impossible
A faulty application could damage kernel state or other processes
Applications would lose all access to memory
questions.answerKey: Kernel-mode code has broad privileges, so application bugs or malicious code can compromise system integrity.
questions.explanation: Possible overhead savings do not eliminate the loss of privilege isolation.

questions.prompt: Trace the mode changes when a user program calls a conventional system-call wrapper, the kernel performs the request, and control returns normally.
questions.answerKey: Execution begins in user mode. The system-call entry mechanism transfers control to a kernel handler in kernel mode; after handling the request, the return path restores user-mode execution. The process does not retain kernel privileges because the entry and return mechanisms control the privilege transition.
questions.explanation: Require the correct sequence and an explanation of why kernel privilege is temporary.
